3.3.1.examLens: Set up the hypotheses, make the decision from a p-value or interval, and word the conclusion correctly.

worked.question: A supplier claims a mean of 50. A sample of 25 gives x̄ = 52 and s = 5. Test H0: μ = 50 against Ha: μ not equal to 50 at α = 0.05. Confirm with a confidence interval.
worked.solution:
t = (52 − 50) ÷ (5 ÷ √25) = 2 ÷ 1 = 2.0, with df = 24. The two-tailed critical value (0.975 column) is 2.064. Since 2.0 is below 2.064, fail to reject H0 (p is about 0.057, above 0.05).
Interval: 52 ± 2.064 × 1 = 49.94 to 54.06. It includes 50, so the conclusion agrees.

3.3.2.examLens: A p-value says a difference is detectable. It does not say the difference matters.

worked.question: (A) Two production lines are compared with 50,000 units each. The mean difference is 0.002 mm, p = 0.0001, tolerance ±0.5 mm. (B) Two training methods are compared with 6 people each. The mean difference is 5 minutes on a 30-minute task, p = 0.12. What do you conclude for each?
worked.solution:
(A) Statistically significant, not practically significant. The difference is far inside the tolerance, so no action is justified.
(B) Inconclusive. A 5-minute difference could matter, but 6 per group gives little power. Collect more data (compute the sample size needed) before deciding.

3.3.3.examLens: Name the error from a story, and know what raises or lowers power.

worked.question: (a) A team concludes a new supplier's parts are stronger. In truth they are identical. Which error? (b) A team concludes a new method is no faster, but it truly is. Which error? (c) If α is lowered from 0.05 to 0.01 with the same sample size, what happens to power?
worked.solution: (a) Type I. (b) Type II. (c) Power decreases. Making it harder to reject H0 lowers the chance of detecting a real difference, unless you increase the sample size.

3.3.4.examLens: "Which test?" is core exam content. Learn the decision order and the tree below, then drill it until it is automatic. SG-3.4 and SG-3.5 give the calculations.

worked.question:
Name the test (assume data are normal unless told otherwise):

  1. Mean fill weight of one sample against a 500 g target.
  2. Mean cycle time of two machines producing different parts.
  3. The same 12 operators timed before and after training.
  4. Mean strength from four suppliers.
  5. Did the variation decrease after a process change (two samples)?
  6. Cycle times (strongly skewed) from three shifts.
  7. Defective rate before versus after a change.
  8. Defect type counts by shift.
  9. Skewed repair times from two lines.
worked.solution: 1. 1-sample t. 2. 2-sample t. 3. Paired t. 4. One-way ANOVA. 5. F test for two variances. 6. Kruskal-Wallis (or Mood's median). 7. 2-proportion test. 8. Chi-square contingency. 9. Mann-Whitney.

3.3.1.a.title: The hypotheses
3.3.1.a.html:
• H0 (null): no difference, no effect, the status quo, equality.
  • Ha (alternative): what you are looking for evidence of. It can be "not equal" (two-sided), "less than," or "greater than."

You never prove the alternative. You collect evidence against the null.

3.3.1.b.title: The steps
3.3.1.b.html:
1. State the practical problem.
  2. State H0 and Ha.
  3. Choose the risk level (α, often 0.05).
  4. Choose the test.
  5. Decide the sample size.
  6. Collect the data.
  7. Compute the test statistic and the p-value.
  8. Make the decision (reject or fail to reject H0).
  9. State the practical conclusion.

3.3.1.c.title: The p-value
3.3.1.c.html: The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if H0 were true. If p is below α, reject H0. Memory aid: low p, null must go.

3.3.1.d.title: Wording the conclusion
3.3.1.d.html: Never say "accept H0." Say "fail to reject H0." A failure to reject means you did not find enough evidence, not that the null is proven.

3.3.1.e.title: One-tailed or two-tailed; independent or paired
3.3.1.e.html:
• Two-tailed: you care about a difference in either direction. One-tailed: you care about only one direction, stated in advance.
  • Independent samples: two separate groups. Paired samples: the same units measured twice (before and after) or matched pairs.

3.3.1.f.title: Confidence intervals and tests agree
3.3.1.f.html: If a 95% confidence interval for the difference excludes the hypothesized value (often zero), a two-sided test at α = 0.05 rejects H0. If the interval includes it, the test fails to reject.

3.3.1.g.title: Careful with the wording
3.3.1.g.html: With p = 0.08 and α = 0.05, you fail to reject H0. The correct statement is "there is not enough evidence of a difference at the 5% level," not "there is no difference."

3.3.2.a.title: Huge samples find tiny differences
3.3.2.a.html: With a very large sample, even a trivial difference can produce a tiny p-value. It is statistically significant without being important.

3.3.2.b.title: Small samples miss big differences
3.3.2.b.html: With a small sample, a large and real difference can fail to reach significance because there is too little data.

3.3.2.c.title: Effect size
3.3.2.c.html: The effect size is the size of the difference, often relative to the variation. The minimum detectable difference is the smallest difference you care about finding.

3.3.2.d.title: Practical significance
3.3.2.d.html: Ask: does the difference matter to the customer, the process, or the business? That question is separate from the p-value.

3.3.2.e.title: Significant but not important
3.3.2.e.html: p = 0.001, but the difference is 0.01 mm and the tolerance is ±0.5 mm. It is statistically significant but not practically significant. Do not re-tool the process because of it.

3.3.2.f.title: Not significant, but not proven the same
3.3.2.f.html: p = 0.07 with a small sample and a large observed effect. The correct reading is "insufficient evidence; check power and sample size," not "no difference."

3.3.3.a.title: Type I error (α)
3.3.3.a.html: Rejecting a true H0. A false alarm: you conclude there is a difference when there is none. Its probability is α.

3.3.3.b.title: Type II error (β)
3.3.3.b.html:
Failing to reject a false H0. A missed detection: a real difference goes unnoticed. Its probability is β.

H0 is trueH0 is false
Reject H0Type I error (α)Correct decision (power = 1 − β)
Fail to reject H0Correct decision (1 − α)Type II error (β)

3.3.3.c.title: Power
3.3.3.c.html: Power = 1 − β, the chance of detecting a real difference. Typical values: α = 0.05 and power of 0.80 to 0.90.

3.3.3.d.title: What raises power
3.3.3.d.html:
• A larger sample size
  • A larger real effect
  • A larger α (at the cost of more false alarms)
  • Less variation

3.3.3.e.title: Confidence level
3.3.3.e.html: Confidence level = 1 − α. A 5% α gives 95% confidence.

3.3.3.f.title: Name the error
3.3.3.f.html: "Concluding the new process is better when it is not" is a Type I error. "Concluding there is no improvement when there actually is" is a Type II error.

3.3.3.g.title: Producer's and consumer's risk
3.3.3.g.html: The names producer's risk (α) and consumer's risk (β) come from acceptance-sampling language. The Type I and Type II definitions are the primary ones.

3.3.4.a.title: What selection depends on
3.3.4.a.html: The right test depends on data type, number of groups, whether groups are independent, paired, or blocked, the parameter being compared (mean or median, variance, proportion), and normality.

3.3.4.b.title: Normal data, means
3.3.4.b.html:
• One sample versus a target: 1-sample t (or Z if σ is known).
  • Two independent groups: 2-sample t.
  • Two paired measurements: paired t.
  • Three or more groups: one-way ANOVA.

3.3.4.c.title: Normal data, variances
3.3.4.c.html:
• One sample versus a target variance: chi-square test for a variance.
  • Two variances: F test.
  • Several variances: Bartlett (needs normality) or Levene (robust to non-normality).

3.3.4.d.title: Non-normal data, medians
3.3.4.d.html:
• One sample versus a target: 1-sample sign or 1-sample Wilcoxon.
  • Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney.
  • Three or more independent groups: Kruskal-Wallis (or Mood's median).
  • Blocked or repeated measures: Friedman.

3.3.4.e.title: Discrete data
3.3.4.e.html:
• One proportion versus a target: 1-proportion test.
  • Two proportions: 2-proportion test.
  • Association between categorical variables: chi-square contingency table.

3.3.4.f.title: Parametric versus non-parametric
3.3.4.f.html: Parametric tests (t, ANOVA) assume a distribution. Non-parametric tests use ranks or signs and assume less. They often have lower power when the parametric model really does hold. The BOK separates normal-data testing (3.4) from non-normal-data testing (3.5), so the exam's default fork is normal versus non-normal. Robustness points (a t-test with a large sample, shape assumptions for rank tests) are refinements on top of that.

3.3.4.g.title: The "which test?" question
3.3.4.g.html: Read the scenario for the clues. The tree below turns the clues into a test.

3.3.4.h.title: The decision order
3.3.4.h.html:
1. Data type: continuous or discrete?
  2. How many groups: one, two, or three or more?
  3. Structure: independent, paired, or blocked?
  4. Parameter: mean or median, variance, or proportion?
  5. Normality: decides parametric versus non-parametric.

Then check sample size and robustness.

3.3.1-1.stem: A hypothesis test returns p = 0.03, and α = 0.05. What is the decision?
3.3.1-1.explanation: p is below α, so reject H0. Memory aid: low p, null must go.

3.3.1-2.stem: A test returns p = 0.12 at α = 0.05. Which conclusion is worded correctly?

options.html: We accept the null hypothesis and conclude the means are equal
We fail to reject the null hypothesis; there is not enough evidence of a difference
We prove there is no difference

3.3.1-2.explanation: Never "accept H0." Failing to reject means there was not enough evidence, not that H0 is proven.

3.3.1-3.stem: A 95% confidence interval for the difference between two means is −0.5 to 3.2. What does this say about a two-sided test at α = 0.05?

options.html: Reject H0, because the interval is wide
Fail to reject H0, because the interval contains zero
Reject H0, because the upper limit is positive

3.3.1-3.explanation: An interval that includes zero is consistent with no difference, so the test fails to reject.

3.3.1-4.stem: The null hypothesis usually states that there is no difference or no effect.
3.3.1-4.explanation: H0 is the status quo or equality. The alternative is the claim you are looking for evidence of.

3.3.1-5.stem: A team will adopt a new method only if it is faster than the current one and wants to test just that direction. Which alternative hypothesis fits?

options.html: The new mean time equals the old mean time
The new mean time is not equal to the old mean time
The new mean time is less than the old mean time
The new mean time is greater than or equal to the old mean time

3.3.1-5.explanation: A claim in one direction is a one-tailed alternative.

3.3.2-1.stem: Two machines are compared with 40,000 parts each. The mean difference is 0.01 mm with p = 0.0004, and the tolerance is ±0.50 mm. What should the team recommend?

options.html: Re-tool immediately, because the result is significant
The difference is statistically significant but not practically significant, so no action is needed
The test is invalid because the sample is too large

3.3.2-1.explanation: A huge sample detects tiny differences. A difference of 0.01 mm inside a ±0.50 mm tolerance does not matter to the customer.

3.3.2-2.stem: Two training methods are compared with 6 people each. The mean difference is 5 minutes on a 30-minute task, with p = 0.07. What is the best response?

options.html: There is no difference between the methods
The evidence is insufficient; check power and collect more data

3.3.2-2.explanation: With a small sample and a potentially important effect, "not significant" does not mean "no difference." Check power and sample size.

3.3.2-3.stem: With a very large sample, even a trivial difference can be statistically significant.
3.3.2-3.explanation: Large samples have high power, so tiny differences can produce small p-values.

3.3.3-1.stem: A team concludes that a new supplier's parts are stronger, but in truth they are identical. Which error occurred?
3.3.3-1.explanation: Rejecting a true null (a false alarm) is a Type I error.

3.3.3-2.stem: A team concludes that a new method is not faster, but it truly is. Which error occurred?
3.3.3-2.explanation: Failing to detect a real difference is a Type II error.

3.3.3-3.stem: If β = 0.10, the power of the test is 0.90.

3.3.3-4.stem: Which TWO changes would increase the power of a test?

options.html: Increase the variation in the data
Reduce the variation in the data

3.3.3-4.explanation: More data and less variation both make a real difference easier to detect. More variation or a smaller effect lowers power.

3.3.3-5.stem: A team lowers α from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing the sample size. What happens to the power?
3.3.3-5.explanation: A stricter α makes it harder to reject H0, which lowers the chance of detecting a real difference.

3.3.4-1.stem: When choosing a hypothesis test, which question should be answered first?

options.html: Is the data continuous or discrete?

3.3.4-1.explanation: The decision order starts with data type, then number of groups, independent or paired, the parameter, and normality.

3.3.4-2.stem: The same 12 operators are timed before and after training, and the times are normal. Which test?
3.3.4-2.explanation: The same units measured twice calls for a paired t-test.

3.3.4-3.stem: The mean cycle times of two machines making different parts are compared, with normal data and no pairing. Which test?
3.3.4-3.explanation: Two independent groups of normal data compared on the mean use the 2-sample t-test.

3.3.4-4.stem: The mean strength of material from four suppliers is compared, with normal data. Which test?
3.3.4-4.explanation: Three or more groups of normal data compared on the mean use one-way ANOVA.

3.3.4-5.stem: After a process change, a team wants to know whether the variation decreased. Both samples are normal. Which test?
3.3.4-5.explanation: A question about variation calls for a variance test, not a mean test.

3.3.4-6.stem: Repair times from two lines are strongly skewed with small samples. Which test compares them?

3.3.4-7.stem: Lead times from three shifts are strongly skewed. Which test compares them?
3.3.4-7.explanation: Three or more independent non-normal groups use Kruskal-Wallis (or Mood's median if outliers matter).

3.3.4-8.stem: The defective rate before a change (30 of 300) is compared with the rate after (18 of 300). Which test?
3.3.4-8.explanation: Comparing two proportions calls for a 2-proportion test.

3.3.4-9.stem: A team counts defect types by shift and wants to know whether defect type depends on shift. Which test?
3.3.4-9.explanation: Counts classified by two categorical variables use a chi-square contingency test.

3.3.4-10.stem: Variances of four groups are compared, and the data are not normal. Which test is appropriate?
3.3.4-10.explanation: Levene's test is robust to non-normal data. Bartlett's test assumes normality.

3.3.3-1.text: A team concludes a new supplier's parts are stronger, but they are identical.
3.3.3-1.answer: Type I error (rejecting a true null; a false alarm).

3.3.3-2.text: A team concludes a new method is no faster, but it truly is faster.
3.3.3-2.answer: Type II error (failing to reject a false null; a missed detection).

3.3.3-3.text: A test rejects H0 and H0 is in fact false.
3.3.3-3.answer: A correct decision; this is what power measures.

3.3.3-4.text: A test fails to reject H0 and H0 is in fact true.

3.3.3-5.text: A test has β = 0.15. What is its power?

3.3.3-6.text: A team lowers α from 0.05 to 0.01 without changing the sample size. What happens to the power?
3.3.3-6.answer: Power decreases, because rejecting H0 is now harder.

3.3.4-1.text: Which hypothesis test fits? The same 15 machines are timed before and after maintenance; the differences are approximately normal.

3.3.4-2.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Mean fill weights of two filling lines are compared; the data are normal and independent.

3.3.4-3.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Mean tensile strength is compared across five suppliers; the data are normal.

3.3.4-4.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Did the variation of cycle time differ between two shifts? Both samples are normal.

3.3.4-5.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Median repair times of two technicians are compared; the data are strongly skewed.

3.3.4-6.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Lead times from four warehouses are skewed and independent.

3.3.4-7.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Three groups have severe outliers, and a robust comparison of medians is wanted.

3.3.4-8.text: Which hypothesis test fits? The same 8 reviewers each rate 4 designs on an ordinal scale; ratings are not normal.

3.3.4-9.text: Which hypothesis test fits? The defect rate before a change is compared with the rate after.

3.3.4-10.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Is defect type independent of machine, using counts?

3.3.4-11.text: Which hypothesis test fits? A sample median is compared with a target; the data are skewed and cannot be assumed symmetric.

3.3.4-12.text: Which hypothesis test fits? A sample median is compared with a target; the distribution is roughly symmetric.

3.3.4-13.text: Which hypothesis test fits? One normal sample's mean is compared with a target; σ is unknown.

3.3.4-14.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Does a process variance exceed a target value? The data are normal.

3.3.4-15.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Are the variances of four groups equal? The data are not normal.

3.3.4-16.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Are the variances of four groups equal? The data are normal.

3.3.4-17.text: Which hypothesis test fits? One proportion defective is compared with a claimed value; counts are large.

3.3.4-18.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Two proportions are compared, but expected counts are very small.

3.3.4-19.text: Which hypothesis test fits? A sample mean is compared with a target and the population σ is known.

3.3.4-20.text: Which hypothesis test fits? Cycle times for the same 12 jobs are measured before and after a change; the differences are skewed.
